title: Standing, sitting, lying down
hook: those who remember Allah in every posture and reflect on creation: You did not make this in vain (3:190–191)

segments.voice: Yesterday: dha'iqa, every soul will taste death, and the world as provision for a journey. Your line was every soul tastes it.

A boy named Ibn Abbas, the Prophet's young cousin, once spent the night at the house of his aunt Maymunah, one of the Prophet's wives. He had come, the reports say, to see how the Prophet ﷺ prayed at night. In the last part of the night, he saw him get up, look at the sky, and begin to recite. Bukhari records what he recited: the last verses of Al 'Imran. Today the surah ends with them, under the same sky.
screen: `A BOY AWAKE AT NIGHT.` → `THE PROPHET LOOKS AT THE SKY.` → `THE LAST VERSES OF AL 'IMRAN.`

segments.voice: Verse 190 says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, there are signs for people of understanding. Verse 191 says who they are: those who remember God standing, sitting, and lying on their sides, and reflect on the creation of the heavens and the earth. And what they say, in Pickthall's words: "Our Lord! Thou createdst not this in vain." Then: glory be to You, protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Three postures cover almost every moment of a human life: work, rest, sleep, sickness. Remembrance isn't tied to one position or one hour. The same three show up in a hadith about prayer. A sick companion asked how to pray, and the Prophet told him: standing; if you can't, then sitting; if you can't, then on your side. Nobody is too weak to be counted. Then the second act: reflection, tafakkur. Not just looking at the stars, but thinking until a conclusion comes out of your mouth: You didn't make this in vain. Batil, the word for in vain, means empty, pointless, false. The people in the verse look at the night sky and conclude the opposite. So the surah that began with clear and ambiguous verses ends here, after the chosen family, Maryam, the rope, Uhud and its grief, and death tasted: a person under the night sky, in whatever posture they can manage, saying: not in vain.
screen: `SIGNS IN NIGHT AND DAY` · `STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `TAFAKKUR: THINKING IT THROUGH` · `BATIL: EMPTY, POINTLESS` · then, large: `THOU CREATEDST NOT THIS IN VAIN.`

segments.voice: Choose your posture, stand, sit or lie down, whichever your body wants, and picture the night sky: the dark, the scattered lights, the distances. Let the size of it settle on you until one thought forms slowly, the way it did for the people in the verse: this is not pointless. If you pray, you can say the verse's own words: Our Lord, You did not create this in vain.
Standing. Standing, sitting, and lying down: remembering God in every posture, and reflecting on creation, from 3:191. Today's word.
Your line: not in vain. Any posture will do. That's Al 'Imran, start to finish.

howItsDone: Some Muslims recite the last verses of Al 'Imran (3:190–200) when they wake for the night prayer, following the Prophet's practice reported in Sahih al-Bukhari, and remember God in whatever posture they're in throughout the day.

chat.says: Can someone who's sick and stuck in bed still remember God?
options: Yes: 3:191 praises remembering God standing, sitting, and lying on your side.
Only once they're well enough to stand, since posture is required.
No: remembrance only counts at the set prayer times in a mosque.
chat.meaning: 3:191 praises those who remember God standing, sitting and lying on their sides; a hadith gives the sick the same three postures for prayer.
